page: Microsoft Azure E48pds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine powered by an arm64-based Microsoft Neoverse-N2 processor running at 3.4 GHz. The instance provisions 48 dedicated physical cores across 48 vCPUs with a single thread per core topology, eliminating resource contention from simultaneous multithreading. It features 64 KB of L1 data cache per core, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and a large shared 128 MB L3 cache. Memory capacity is configured at 384.0 GB of RAM, yielding an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio (8.0 GB per core). For high-speed temporary storage, the instance bundles 2835 GB of local NVMe SSD capacity. It does not include hardware GPU acceleration or complimentary public IPv4 addresses, and hypervisor management is handled via Microsoft Hyper-V.

Benchmark outcomes show distinct throughput strengths tied to its memory subsystem and core scaling. The instance delivers top-tier memory bandwidth, recording 463.82 GB/sec for uncached 256 MB reads and 199.65 GB/sec for uncached writes, corroborated by a top-tier PassMark memory score of 3391.3. Multi-threaded execution is strong, evidenced by a Geekbench multi-core score of 21816.0 (top 10%) and 99354.67 on stress-ng multi-core tests. Database and caching benchmarks demonstrate notable performance, yielding a top-tier PassMark database operations score of 37978.53 and 89.5 million Redis SET operations per second. In contrast, single-core metrics fall into average percentiles, including a 1692.0 Geekbench single-core score and 2073.49 in single-threaded stress-ng.

Cost efficiency is driven by the density of the 64-bit ARM architecture paired with generous memory allocation and integrated NVMe storage. Because the instance utilizes native ARM cores without hyperthreading, users gain predictable performance per vCPU for parallelized in-memory workloads without paying the premium typically associated with standard x86 architectures. A primary engineering trade-off is the absence of x86-specific instruction sets like AVX, AVX-512, and AMX, alongside lower throughput on massive sequential compute tasks such as large-model LLM prompt processing (6.9 tokens/sec on 70B models). The server is best suited for memory-intensive relational databases, in-memory key-value caches like Redis, big data processing pipelines, and parallelized compilation tasks.
